Article Title: Russia to send first diesel shipment to US on Thursday amid global supply crunch
Article Text: Russia will send its first 40,000-tonne diesel shipment to the United States on Thursday, under an agreement with President Donald Trump to resume Russian fuel supplies, Russia's deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said.The move comes as global diesel markets face a supply squeeze, while Ukraine has warned that renewed Russian energy exports could help finance Moscow's war effort.According to Reuters, Novak said further shipments would follow the agreement between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump, adding that Moscow would meet US demand within its capabilities. The first cargo is part of a broader supply plan announced by President Trump.Trump has announced plans for Russia to supply 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel initially, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another 1 million tonnes thereafter. The arrangement is aimed at increasing fuel supplies amid a global diesel shortage and rising prices.Russia had imposed a ban on diesel exports after Ukrainian drone strikes on its oil refineries disrupted production and caused fuel shortages in the country.On October 9, Moscow lifted the ban, allowing Russian suppliers to resume diesel shipments to international markets.The development comes after US President Donald Trump pushed for a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine targeting attacks on energy infrastructure. The proposed arrangement aimed to halt strikes on oil refineries, power facilities and other energy sites, as attacks on critical infrastructure disrupted fuel supplies and added pressure on energy markets.Ukraine has opposed easing restrictions on Russian energy exports, arguing that additional revenue from diesel sales could help Moscow finance its war effort.President Volodymyr Zelensky criticised the US-Russia arrangement, warning that allowing Russia to expand fuel exports while the war continues could weaken pressure on the Kremlin to end the conflict.Europe is also facing growing pressure on diesel supplies as disruptions to Middle Eastern exports tighten the market. Reuters reported in September that the disruption had cut Europe's diesel and jet fuel supplies by about a quarter, pushing fuel inventories to a 12-year low.Nigeria's Dangote refinery has increased exports to Europe to help fill the gap, highlighting the region's growing reliance on alternative suppliers.Reuters reported on October 21 that analysts expect the US-Russia diesel deal to have limited impact on global fuel prices, as the promised supplies may be too small to ease the market shortage. Analysts also questioned whether Russia could meet the announced export targets given damage to its refineries and rising shipping costs.With EU restrictions limiting direct imports of Russian fuel, the additional supplies are unlikely to provide an immediate solution to Europe's diesel concerns.
Article Summary: Russia will send its first 40,000-tonne diesel shipment to the United States on Thursday. The move comes as global diesel markets face a supply squeeze. Russia had imposed a ban on diesel exports after Ukrainian drone strikes on its oil refineries disrupted production and caused fuel shortages.

Article Title: Playing doubles with AI: How human judgement becomes the winning partner
Article Text:
Industry leaders at Elevate Connect London emphasized the need for human judgement in AI adoption and implementation

‘AI should complement human capabilities’

Business context and governance key to scaling AI

How much Data Quality is enough for AI?

Polar explorer draws parallels with business leadership

LONDON: As businesses accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), industry leaders have stressed the importance of human judgement, trusted data and strong governance in turning technological capabilities into meaningful business outcomes.The issue was central to Elevate Connect London 2026, the flagship event organised by Mumbai-based IT multinational ADROSONIC for senior leaders in the UK insurance market. Held at the Four Seasons Hotel London at Tower Bridge, the invitation-only gathering focused on the theme “AI Predicts. Humans Decide.”Discussions covered AI adoption, data quality, business transformation and leadership, with speakers emphasising that technology alone cannot deliver value without human expertise and organisational readiness.One of the key sessions was a fireside conversation titled “Playing Doubles with AI”, featuring Mayank, founder and CEO of ADROSONIC, and Hasani Jess, group CTO of Aventum Group.Drawing on the example of tennis legend Leander Paes, Mayank compared effective human-AI collaboration to a doubles partnership, where complementary strengths matter more than identical capabilities.“Great doubles partnerships are not built by finding someone identical to you,” Mayank said.“They are built by combining complementary strengths and compensating for one another’s weaknesses.”He cited Paes’s career to illustrate how ambition, context and human judgement can defy expectations based solely on data. While AI can process information, conduct research and improve efficiency, people must interpret that information and decide how to act on it.Jess said effective AI use requires practice and expertise, despite the technology’s apparent accessibility.“AI is intoxicatingly familiar,” he said. “It looks easy because we can all interact with it. But just as watching a professional athlete is very different from performing at that level, working effectively with AI requires discipline, learning and experience.”The speakers also discussed the importance of trust, noting that confidence in AI systems must develop through repeated use and demonstrated reliability. With models evolving rapidly, organisations must continually reassess how best to combine human and machine capabilities.For Mayank, the real opportunity lies in using AI to achieve outcomes that would otherwise be beyond an organisation’s reach.“If AI is only helping us do the same things faster, that is one plus one equals two,” he said. “The real opportunity comes when AI enables us to do things we could not do before. That is when one plus one becomes eleven.”Another panel examined how businesses can expand AI adoption while protecting human expertise, governance and client trust.James Welch, head of delivery at Miller, said AI deployment must reflect the risks associated with individual business functions.While high-risk areas such as claims and payments require strong human oversight, tasks such as generating renewal packs could benefit significantly from automation. He added that protecting the company’s brand, expertise and client relationships remained a priority.Nitin Agrawal, lead business architect at ADROSONIC, said adoption, rather than technology, was often the biggest challenge.He stressed the need to redesign operating models, upskill employees and involve business users in developing AI initiatives.Daniel Del Moro, director of AI and automation innovation at UiPath, highlighted the importance of reliable data and well-defined processes.He cautioned against treating AI as a cure-all, arguing that businesses must first address process inefficiencies and data-quality problems. Combining established technologies such as robotic process automation (RPA) with newer AI tools could help unlock greater value, he said.The panel’s broader message was that AI adoption should be treated as a business transformation programme, supported by leadership, change management, clear accountability and end-to-end objectives, rather than as an isolated technology project.Data readiness was another focus, with leaders from AUB Group, Hampden Risk Partners, Oneglobal Broking and ADROSONIC discussing how businesses can establish reliable data foundations without delaying AI projects in pursuit of perfect information.The panel agreed that data should be trustworthy, understood and fit for the decision it is intended to support.Raj Rai said competitive advantage would depend not merely on adopting AI, but on understanding data quality, lineage, governance and how the technology is applied within an organisation.Ben Ormerod noted that the level of data quality required depends on the decision being made. Although AI can accelerate business outcomes, poor-quality inputs can also speed up poor decisions. He also highlighted AI’s potential to identify data-quality issues and trace data lineage.Marc Steel said AI should support rather than replace human expertise, particularly in relationship-driven sectors such as specialty insurance, where client relationships and market context remain important.Kamlesh Yadav cautioned that confidence expressed by AI systems should not be mistaken for accuracy. He emphasised the need for trusted information, clear ownership, human oversight and measurable business outcomes.The discussion highlighted the need to balance experimentation with safeguards, ensuring that innovation does not come at the expense of security, accountability or sound decision-making.The event also featured a keynote by polar explorer Ann Daniels, who drew on her expeditions across the Arctic and Antarctica to discuss leadership, resilience and decision-making under uncertainty.Daniels described operating in environments where conditions can change without warning, resources are limited and decisions can have serious consequences. In such situations, success depends on preparation, teamwork and the ability to adapt when plans no longer work.Her experiences offered parallels with the challenges facing businesses as AI capabilities, market expectations and competitive pressures evolve. Just as polar explorers must reassess conditions and adjust their routes, business leaders must make decisions without always having complete information.Daniels emphasised that technology and data can support decisions, but leaders still need to judge when and how to act on the information available. Her keynote reinforced the event’s broader focus on adaptability, collaboration and human judgement during periods of change.A Boardroom Live session also examined a proposal to expand ADROSONIC’s Digital Innovation Lab at BIT Mesra.Across the sessions, speakers returned to a common theme: AI’s value depends not only on what the technology can do, but also on the quality of the data, processes and decisions surrounding it.As organisations move beyond experimentation, effective adoption will require combining technological capability with human expertise, clear governance and trust.
Article Summary: Industry leaders emphasise the need for human judgement in AI adoption and implementation. The issue was central to Elevate Connect London 2026, the flagship event organised by Mumbai-based IT multinational ADROSONIC. Discussions covered AI adoption, data quality, business transformation and leadership.

Article Title: 'Can't compromise data': Malaysia bans civil servants from using Waze, citing links to Israel
Article Text:
Malaysia has barred civil servants from using Waze over data security concerns linked to its Israeli origins

Malaysia has banned civil servants from using Alphabet-owned navigation app Waze, citing concerns over data security linked to the app's Israeli origins, following a review ordered by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.The prohibition took effect immediately, according to a letter dated Tuesday from chief secretary to the overnment Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar to heads of government agencies.Anwar said the government was examining potential security risks associated with Waze, which he said “was bound to Israeli laws”.“We cannot compromise on the security of people's data and identities,” news agency Reuters quoted Anwar saying in a Facebook post after chairing a meeting of the national cybersecurity committee on Tuesday.The prime minister did not specify the security risks identified but recommended that government employees use TuJu, a domestic mapping application developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority, as an alternative.Waze, founded in Israel, provides real-time traffic updates using satellite signals and data crowdsourced from drivers. Google parent Alphabet acquired the app in 2013 for about $1 billion.The decision comes against the backdrop of Malaysia's strong support for the Palestinian cause. The Muslim-majority country does not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
Article Summary: Malaysia bans civil servants from using Google-owned navigation app Waze. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim cites concerns over data security linked to app's Israeli origins. Waze provides real-time traffic updates using satellite signals and data crowdsourced from drivers.

Article Title: SpaceX profits skyrocket to $4.4 billion as revenue jumps 161%, AI business surges 830%
Article Text:
SpaceX revenue surges 161% to $14.6 billion in Q3

Starlink adds 1.6 million subscribers in three months

Computing capacity expands as investment climbs

SpaceX's Super Intelligence business has become the biggest driver of the company's latest quarterly growth, helping Elon Musk's aerospace company report a net profit of $4.4 billion in the July-September quarter.Revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, rising 161 per cent to $14.6 billion, while spending on infrastructure also increased sharply.The company's third-quarter results showed a turnaround from the year-ago period, when SpaceX recorded a net loss of $1.1 billion on revenue of $5.6 billion. Adjusted EBITDA, which measures operating performance, rose 306 per cent to $8.8 billion from $2.2 billion.The Super Intelligence (SI) business, covering computing infrastructure, models and software applications, generated $7.6 billion in revenue during the quarter. This was an 830 per cent increase from $813 million in the corresponding period last year.SpaceX said the segment added $6.7 billion in year-on-year revenue through its solutions and infrastructure. Growth was attributed to new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor and wider adoption of Grok products by enterprise customers and consumers.Connectivity services, led by Starlink, remained another major source of revenue for SpaceX.The segment brought in $5.2 billion in the quarter, marking a 69 per cent increase from $3.1 billion a year earlier. Its operating income rose 99 per cent to $2.4 billion.Starlink's consumer subscriber base reached 13.6 million as of September 30, compared with 7.2 million a year earlier. It added 1.6 million subscribers during the quarter. Monthly average revenue per user rose to $69 from $66 in the previous quarter.Space-related activities contributed $1.8 billion in revenue, up 6 per cent year-on-year. SpaceX completed 12 customer launches during the July-September period.The company also reported that its first orbital Starship flight delivered 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The deployment added around 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch.SpaceX's expansion came with a steep rise in capital spending. Capital expenditure stood at $19.6 billion in the third quarter, against $6.9 billion in the same period last year, largely due to investment in computing infrastructure.The company's computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts by September 30, compared with 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier, as it continued building infrastructure for its Super Intelligence business.The chief financial officer said the company intended to pursue expansion while keeping its investments and balance sheet on a disciplined footing."We are building the infrastructure of the future with discipline--focused on capital efficiency, strong returns on invested capital, and maintaining a robust, investment-grade balance sheet--while moving with the velocity to capture the opportunity in front of us," the CFO said.
Article Summary: SpaceX revenue surges 161% to $14.6 billion in Q3. Starlink adds 1.6 million subscribers in three months. Super Intelligence business adds $6.7 billion in year-on-year revenue. SpaceX completed 12 customer launches during the July- September period.

Article Title: AI boom set to push Big Tech investment beyond $1 trillion in 2027, says UBS
Article Text:
Tech giants' AI spending to exceed $1 trillion in 2027

AI spending supports US economic growth

Rising investment puts pressure on cash flows

Big tech firms are set to splurge over $1 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027 as demand for computing power continues to grow faster than supply, according to a report by UBS.The investment boom is also helping boost US economic growth, even as companies face rising funding needs. Spending on AI infrastructure is expected to cross $600 billion in 2026 before topping $1 trillion in 2027, the report stated.“Demand has exceeded capacity ahead of schedule,” UBS said, pointing to the growing pressure on companies to expand their computing infrastructure to keep up with demand.It expects spending to rise further over the next year, although the pace of growth could peak in 2027. Higher investment is putting pressure on companies’ cash flows and increasing their need for additional funding.The growing investment in AI infrastructure has become a significant contributor to the US economy. According to UBS, spending on AI infrastructure added around 0.75 percentage points to US gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the first half of 2026.Rising equity prices linked to AI companies have also boosted household wealth and consumption, providing another source of support for economic activity.However, the report found little clear evidence that AI has so far led to a substantial increase in overall productivity or widespread job displacement.Its estimated effect on the overall unemployment rate remains limited, at around 0.2 percentage points or less.The impact on employment has varied across industries. Selected high-technology sectors, including software and computer systems design, recorded a 1.4 per cent year-on-year decline in employment. In contrast, construction industries supporting data centre infrastructure saw employment grow by nearly 3 per cent.While demand for AI infrastructure continues to drive investment, UBS has flagged emerging financing pressures among major technology companies. Their cash flows have weakened as spending has increased, while demand for their bond issuances has become less robust.The report said investors expect free cash flow to return to positive territory in 2028, provided companies are able to generate sufficient revenue from AI services.The ability to convert heavy infrastructure spending into sustainable revenue will therefore remain important as the investment cycle progresses.AI demand is also contributing to higher prices in some areas, including software, digital goods and electricity, according to UBS. However, the report noted that productivity gains from AI could help reduce inflation over time.The outlook for the investment cycle will depend on whether demand for computing power continues to exceed available capacity and whether technology companies can turn their growing investments into sustainable revenue growth.
Article Summary: Spending on AI infrastructure is expected to cross $600 billion in 2026 before topping $1 trillion in 2027. Higher investment is putting pressure on companies’ cash flows and increasing their need for additional funding. Growing investment in AI infrastructure has become a significant contributor to US economy.

Article Title: 24 million barrels a day: Gulf oil flows surge past prewar levels despite US-Iran war
Article Text:
Oil flows from the Middle East have topped prewar levels at over 24 million barrels a day despite escalating attacks on shipping in Hormuz

How oil is moving despite the attacks

Attacks raise the cost of shipping

Iran's leverage over oil flows weakens

Persian Gulf oil exports have climbed above prewar levels despite intensifying attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, as tankers adapt to the risks with US protection and alternative routes help keep supplies moving.Oil flows from the Middle East, including shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending October 18, exceeding the prewar average of 23.3 million barrels a day, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler.However, shipments through the Strait of Hormuz remain below their earlier levels. Preliminary estimates put average flows through the strait, including offshore transfers in the Gulf of Oman, at around 14 million barrels a day during the same period, about 82% of prewar volumes, the Wall Stree Journal reported.The recovery comes as the risks to shipping remain high. Around 30 attacks on vessels have been reported in October, accounting for about 20% of all ship attacks recorded during the war, according to Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a senior analyst at maritime intelligence firm Windward.An improvised shipping system, supported by US protection, has helped tankers continue carrying crude through the high-risk waterway.Some vessels make short trips into the Gulf to load oil before travelling through Hormuz and transferring their cargo to other ships near Oman for onward delivery.Tankers often switch off their tracking signals during parts of these journeys. American air cover provides some protection along a corridor near the Omani coast, although vessels remain vulnerable to attacks.Pipelines running across Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are also helping exporters bypass the strait. Around 40% of non-Iranian crude shipped out of the Gulf in September travelled through routes that avoided Hormuz, compared with 17% before the war, Kpler estimated.“The big picture is that the system for shipping through a dangerous Strait of Hormuz is now well-established and the risk appetite of those involved in exporting oil has risen,” said Hamad Hussain, a senior commodities economist at Capital Economics.The increased willingness to take risks is partly driven by the potential returns. Traders can earn around $20 more per barrel by reselling Iraqi oil than before the war, according to Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis. That translates into an additional $40 million on a supertanker carrying a typical cargo of two million barrels.Shipowners are also offering higher payments to attract crews willing to make the dangerous crossings. One China-based ship-staffing company offered seafarers as much as $25,000 for a round trip that typically takes one or two weeks, The Wall Street Journal reported.“The volumes remain high despite rising attacks, because profits make it worth the risk,” Falakshahi said.The continued movement of oil has not made the route safe. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has used drones and missiles against vessels attempting the crossing, while small boats have also been used to target shipping.The risks were illustrated by the Tanzania-flagged supertanker "Loyalty", which entered the Persian Gulf twice in September and October to load Iraqi crude. After transferring two million barrels of oil to another tanker in the Gulf of Oman in early October, it returned to the Gulf for another cargo.On October 16, the vessel was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat, maritime security company Vanguard said. The projectile damaged a freshwater tank while the tanker was carrying two million barrels of Iraqi crude, according to a crew member.The danger has pushed up the cost of transporting oil. Freight for a supertanker carrying Gulf crude to China approached a record $37.37 per barrel this week, Kpler said. War-risk insurance premiums have risen to as much as 10% of a vessel's value, from less than 3% before the conflict, according to Windward.“In April, the problem was a shortage of crude. In October, it is the cost of moving it,” said Natasha Kaneva, head of the global commodities strategy team at JPMorgan.Brent crude rose to around $108 a barrel on Tuesday, reflecting concerns that the improvement in oil flows may not last if fighting intensifies again. With global inventories thinning, any renewed disruption could leave markets with limited room to absorb a supply shock.The recovery in regional exports contrasts with the pressure on Iran's own oil trade, which has been constrained by a US maritime blockade.Tehran has sought to reassert control over Hormuz, warning that neighbouring countries should not be able to export oil if Iran cannot ship its own. But the continued movement of crude through the strait and alternative routes has weakened its ability to deter regional shipments.“Iran would have to be more aggressive to achieve the same degree of control it previously possessed over oil flows from the region,” Hussain said.That leaves the market facing two competing realities: oil exports have recovered beyond prewar levels, but the cost and danger of moving crude remain elevated. Whether the recovery can be sustained will depend on the security of shipping routes and whether the conflict escalates further.
Article Summary: Oil flows from the Middle East averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending October 18. Around 30 attacks on vessels have been reported in October, accounting for about 20% of all ship attacks recorded during the war. An improvised shipping system, supported by US protection, has helped tankers carry crude through the high-risk waterway.

Article Title: Oil prices today: Brent crude tops $110 as Middle East tensions threaten shipments
Article Text:
Oil prices climb over 1% (representative image)

Tanker attacks raise concerns over oil supplies

Oil prices retreat from five-month high

US works to increase fuel supplies

Oil prices rose on Wednesday as traders weighed concerns over Middle East supplies amid growing risks to shipping in the Red Sea and threats to oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.Brent crude futures climbed $1.34, or 1.23 per cent, to $110.10 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose $1.18, or 1.21 per cent, to $99 per barrel.The gains followed a decline in the previous session, when prices eased after Iran's president discussed mediation efforts with Pakistan's army chief during a meeting in Tehran.Supply concerns intensified after a supertanker caught fire after striking a sea mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy.Iranian media reported that the vessel had been “violating” Iranian regulations.At least 18 vessel attacks were reported over a two-week period, ship-tracking firm Kpler said in a note on Monday.The attacks have also spread beyond the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil shipments.“Attacks on tankers have expanded beyond the Strait of Hormuz,” LSEG analysts said in a note.“Iran has been targeting vessels as far south as the Gulf of Oman, threatening loadings outside of the Arab Gulf, as well as the ship-to-ship transfers that have helped to support Middle East loadings as the conflict has dragged on,” the analysts added.The Houthis on Monday claimed responsibility for attacks on a Saudi Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and the airports in Riyadh and Abha, Saudi Arabia.Meanwhile, the death toll from a Houthi attack on Yemeni government forces on Monday rose to 73 as fighting intensified, Reuters reported.Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said in a television interview aired on Tuesday that Tehran had not received a response from Saudi Arabia or Yemen's Houthis to its offer to help broker peace talks.Despite Wednesday's gains, crude prices had fallen in the previous session after reaching elevated levels.Brent crude futures settled down 76 cents, or 0.69 per cent, at $108.79 per barrel on Tuesday, after touching a five-month high of $111.99.The November contract for US WTI crude, which expired on Tuesday, settled $1.87 lower, down 1.8 per cent, at $101.79 per barrel.In the United States, two Energy Department officials said on Tuesday that they were working with refiners around the world to increase fuel production as a diesel shortage pushed prices higher.US crude oil inventories were also expected to have declined in the week ended October 16, alongside stocks of refined petroleum products, according to an extended Reuters poll.The eight analysts surveyed by Reuters estimated that US crude inventories fell by an average of around 800,000 barrels during the week.Market participants are monitoring developments across the Middle East, including threats to shipping routes and energy infrastructure, for their potential impact on oil supplies and prices.
Article Summary: Brent crude futures climbed $1.34, or 1.23 per cent, to $110.10 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 1.21 per cent to $99 per barrel. The gains followed a decline in the previous session, when prices eased after Iran's president discussed mediation efforts with Pakistan's army chief.

Article Title: Asean emerges as fastest growing region for exports
Article Text:
Since March, countries have recalibrated their energy purchases due to the disruption in West Asia.

European Union Sees Slowest Pace Of Increase In April-Aug

NEW DELHI: It all boils down to one commodity: Oil products. Asean has emerged as the fastest growing region for India’s exports due to a spurt in petro product shipments – mainly to Singapore -- while the European Union saw the slowest pace of increase during AprilAug as export of petroleum products fell.Latest data available with the commerce department showed that India’s exports to Asean went up 56% during the first five months of the fiscal year as oil product shipments soared 2.4 times to over $6.1 billion, with Singapore accounting for almost threefourths of it. What also helped was a 20-fold jump in computer hardware to $1.4 billion to Asean countries and strong growth of electric machinery (82% to $1.6 billion) and buffalo meat (42% to $1 billion)Since March, countries have recalibrated their energy purchases due to the disruption in West Asia.In contrast, when it comes to EU, oil product exports fell 21% to $4.6 billion as the Netherlands cut back on purchases from India. While the Netherlands was the top destination for Indian fuel, with exports of $5.3 billion during April-Aug 2025, it has now slipped to the third place, behind Singapore and Tanzania, as the value of shipments crashed 47% to $2.8 billion.A part of the impact in EU was offset by Spain and Italy. In April-Aug, India’s exports to Spain rose 54% to $3.5 billion, with oil products jumping to $1.1 billion during the period, as against $172 million ayear ago – an over six-fold increase.In case of Italy, the jump was even more dramatic as petroleum product exports rose from $4 million during April-Aug 2025 to $659 million so far this year.Oil exports to North America fell 7% to $1.9 billion and the 8% rise in overall exports to the region, largely the US, was led by iPhones as telecom instruments rose 29% to over $11 billion, accounting for 23.5% of the exports to the region. Pharma exports too fell 5% to just under $4 billion.Exports to the region slowed as the value of shipments to the US was up just over 6% to $42.8 billion, data showed.
Article Summary: Indian exports to Asean went up 56% during the first five months of the fiscal year. Oil product shipments soared 2.4 times to over $6.1 billion, with Singapore accounting for almost threefourths of it. In contrast, when it comes to EU, oil product exports fell 21% to $4.6 billion.

Article Title: Wall Street climbs as healthcare stocks hit record, oil prices ease; Dow Jones up 0.97%, S&P gains 0.42%
Article Text:
Healthcare stocks were among the biggest gainers

Wall Street's main indexes traded higher on Tuesday, with healthcare stocks reaching a record high and easing oil prices supporting sentiment as investors assessed corporate earnings and lingering concerns over artificial intelligence spending.The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.97% to 52,468.06, while the S&P 500 gained 0.42% to 7,723.06. The Nasdaq Composite edged up 0.22% to 26,489.60 as of 12.06 pm ET.Healthcare stocks were among the biggest gainers, with Eli Lilly rising 4.7 per cent to a record high. Amgen, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie each advanced more than 2 per cent. Financial stocks also climbed 1.2 per cent, helping lift the broader market.Oil prices moved lower after an unsettled session in which Brent crude touched a five-month high. Brent futures fell 1.1 per cent as traders assessed reports of attacks on Saudi infrastructure by Yemen's Houthis and vessel attacks in the Gulf. Lower crude prices offered some relief amid concerns over inflation and energy supply disruptions.The gains followed a rebound on Monday, when investors returned to technology stocks after last week's sharp selloff.Concerns over the borrowing costs and debt exposure associated with the artificial intelligence boom have kept markets volatile. CoreWeave shares rose 2.5 per cent on Tuesday, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index advanced 0.7 per cent.Corporate earnings also drove individual stocks. Credit reporting firm Equifax surged 11.4 per cent after posting better-than-expected third-quarter profits, while toy maker Hasbro gained 5.6 per cent after raising its full-year revenue and digital gaming forecasts.Industrial conglomerate 3M rose 5 per cent after expanding its data-centre partnership with Amazon and increasing its annual profit outlook. General Motors dropped 6.9 per cent, however, after warning of pressure from higher commodity costs and weaker truck sales in the coming months. Steel Dynamics fell 1.4 per cent after missing quarterly profit estimates.Investors are looking to a busy earnings calendar for signs that corporate growth can withstand economic uncertainty and the high cost of financing technology investments. Netflix and SpaceX were scheduled to report results after Tuesday's market close, followed by Meta Platforms and Tesla on Wednesday.In Asia, South Korean artificial intelligence infrastructure company Elice Group fell nearly 30% on its stock market debut, trading below its initial public offering price.Market breadth remained positive, with advancing stocks outnumbering decliners by 2.51 to 1 on the New York Stock Exchange and 2.78 to 1 on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 recorded 21 new 52-week highs and one new low, while the Nasdaq Composite posted 32 new highs and 204 new lows.
Article Summary: The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.97% to 52,468.06, while the S&P 500 gained 0.42% to 7,723.06. The Nasdaq Composite edged up 0.22% to 26,489.60 as of 12.06 pm ET. Healthcare stocks were among the biggest gainers, with Eli Lilly rising 4.7% to a record high.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
Article Summary: The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023. India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year. The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion.

Article Title: Startups Revolutionizing Carbon Dioxide into Valuable Products
Article Text: For most perfume makers, ingredients to make it smell great are the most important feature. But for Stafford Sheehan, a cofounder and chemist at Air Company, the most important part of perfume-making has no scent at all.New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. While the pale yellow-color Air Eau de Parfum is about 50% more expensive than Coco Chanel’s signature No. 5, Sheehan says his product is uniquely valuable: Every 50-milliliter bottle uses 3.6 grams of CO2 that otherwise would have been released into the atmosphere. Its package reads: “Turning CO2 into something beautiful.”While the volume of CO2 utilized in the bottle is extremely small, Air Company’s perfume showcases one way the coming wave of captured carbon can be put to use. Renewable energy and electric cars alone won’t be enough to cut CO2 emissions to zero. The world will almost certainly need to capture billions of tons of the gas annually in the coming decades. Large amounts will likely be stored underground.Using it — so-called carbon capture and utilization, or CCU — to create new products from perfume to jet fuel could be an important tool in the fight against climate change, too, though the nascent industry has major hurdles to overcome.Roughly 230 million tons of CO2 are utilized every year, according to a 2019 report by the International Energy Agency. While roughly one-third of that is reused to force more oil from the ground — hardly a carbon-neutral process — CCU advocates say that the number of companies coming up with new uses for carbon has mushroomed in recent years, paving a way to unlock climate benefits. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology and lower costs.Calgary-based CleanO2 transforms CO2 captured from building heating boilers into feedstock to make soap. Newlight Technologies, a biotechnology startup based in California, takes carbon pulled directly from the air and turns it into biodegradable plastics. Germany’s Covestro AG, one of the world’s largest polymer manufacturers, is also switching some of its fossil fuel-based feedstocks to carbon-derived materials for everything ranging from car shells to medical devices and stadium roofs.Most companies working on CO2-sequestering products are still in their infancy. To grow the emerging sector, global venture capitalists in 2022 poured nearly $500 million into carbon utilization businesses, according to the IEA. That’s in stark contrast to 2015, when barely any venture money went to technologies that utilize CO2.“It’s just a whole different landscape today than it was a decade ago,” says Sasha Mackler, executive director of the energy program at Washington, DC-based non-profit Bipartisan Policy Center.Jennifer Holmgren, chief executive officer of LanzaTech Global Inc., has experienced the shifting sentiment firsthand. The Illinois-based company uses a carbon-eating bacteria – discovered in the guts of rabbits and preserved as powder – to make alternative ethanol in bioreactors not dissimilar to how breweries ferment beer. In the early 2010s, when Holmgren touted carbon-derived ethanol to prospective customers, her sales pitch was met with skepticism.But the tide began turning later that decade. In 2018, the company’s jet fuel produced from the emissions of a Chinese steel mill helped power a Transatlantic flight. LanzaTech has also inked agreements with airlines including Japan’s All Nippon Airways to supply CO2-derived jet fuel. And LanzaJet, the company’s spin-off, plans to start producing sustainable jet fuels at a commercial scale this year.Yet for all the hype around sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using captured carbon, the industry is still an extremely small player. Almost every major airline in the world has pledged to use at least 10% sustainable jet fuels by 2030, yet SAF makes up only 0.1% of global aviation fuel supply — and much of it is made from sources other than captured CO2, such as used cooking oil.“There’s a lot more interest because consumers have become much more interested in buying things that are lower carbon,” says Holmgren. That’s enabled LanzaTech to expand the number of products that utilize CO2.American plastic container maker Plastipak, for instance, has partnered with LanzaTech to produce carbon-derived packaging materials, while polyester converted from LanzaTech’s ethanol has replaced its petroleum-based counterpart at a pilot scale in Lululemon shorts, Zara dresses, H&M yoga pants, On running shoes and Craghoppers jackets. Like SAF, though, there’s still a long way to go for CO2-derived polyester to reach meaningful levels of use.Momentum to grow beyond one-off products and low-scale production has also been supercharged by a growing array of regulations and incentives around the world. For instance, the Inflation Reduction Act that US President Joe Biden signed in 2022 raised the tax credit for carbon capture and utilization by more than 70% to $60 per metric ton in an effort to make costly projects more financially appealing.To keep the climate within habitable limits, the IEA estimates that carbon capture will have to grow to 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually by mid-century. CCU will play a role, though just how big remains to be seen. Not every use case is created equal and some approaches, such as dissolving compressed CO2 in water to make carbonated beverages, only store the gas temporarily. To quantify the true climate benefit of carbon utilization, experts say third-party verification is badly needed.The rise of CCU technology comes as another key approach in President Biden’s net-zero roadmap is hitting a bit of a wall. Carbon capture and storage — that is, gathering CO2 as it’s released from a coal-fired power plant or other emissions source and sequestering it underground — has faced challenges because carbon is often captured in one place and stored in another. That requires pipelines to transport the gas, which many local communities have opposed. Blackrock-backed Navigator, for example, recently announced it was scrapping a planned 1,300-mile CO2 pipeline.Carbon utilization companies say that they can sidestep that issue by using carbon near or at where it’s captured.At its 12-acre factory in Brooklyn, Glenwood Mason Supply demonstrates how. The concrete manufacturer takes CO2 captured at a residential building by its partner company, CarbonQuest, and uses a technique licensed from low-carbon concrete startup CarbonCure to convert the compressed carbon into a powder not unlike dry ice. It then injects it into industrial mixers. There, the CO2 meets cement, sand and aggregate, setting off a series of chemical reactions. The final result is concrete blocks with CO2 sealed in.The technique not only stores carbon but it can also make the blocks marginally stronger. The company estimates that it has utilized about 100 tons of CO2 in total since 2020. Even if the blocks break down, the stored carbon won’t be released as CO2 because it’s been mineralized.“Cement is a big offender in carbon emissions,” says Constance Cincotta, founder of the concrete factory. She became intrigued by the technology and its ability to lower her company's climate impact after hearing about it at an industry conference in the early 2010s. But it wasn't until CarbonCure came on the scene a few years ago that the prospect of CO2-storing cement became tangible. Glenwood Mason then sourced CO2 locally from CarbonQuest, which captures carbon from buildings in New York. Those factors have enabled large-scale production.While Cincotta’s intended to help the planet, she and her team discovered that sinking CO2 into concrete blocks is good for the business, too. In 2019, New York City — where the majority of the company’s concrete blocks are sold — passed a regulation requiring all buildings to shrink their carbon footprint 40% by the end of the decade. Glenwood Mason’s phones have been ringing ever since, with calls from architects and property developers who want to leverage their lower-carbon building materials to cut emissions, says Jeff Hansen, the company’s vice president in architectural sales and marketing.The factory’s CO2-storing concrete blocks also caught the eye of Amazon.com Inc, which in 2022 persuaded a real estate developer to purchase roughly 50,000 blocks for the construction of a new warehouse in New York that Amazon has leased. Had Glenwood Mason not sealed CO2 in its blocks, it wouldn’t have won the contract, Hansen says. To figure out how to pack more carbon into its products, the company has set up a laboratory in its factory to test the reaction between CO2 and other concrete feedstocks under different temperatures and humidity levels.But figuring out the right formula is only one consideration. Utilizing CO2 often comes with an additional cost. As the demand for CO2-derived products climbs, that green premium is expected to go down. Yet “it’s very hard to be a cost parity with a 100-year-old industry that doesn’t even have to pay for its externalities,” says Holmgren of LanzaTech. Even with economies of scale, Holmgren estimates that carbon-containing fabrics will still likely cost as much as 20% higher than conventional ones.“It’s unlikely that we will ever be a cost parity,” she says.In addition to the cost barrier, CCU companies also have to convince end users that may be suspicious of unproven new technologies.Changing feedstocks “does come with risks,” says Keith Wiggins, chief executive officer of Econic Technologies, a British startup that specializes in making carbon-derived chemicals. To get risk-averse industries onboard, Wiggins says his company is laser-focused on those that are under consumer pressure to change course.That strategy seems to be working. Econic has teamed up with three manufacturers in the US, China and India to produce mattresses, outdoor garments and building insulation materials that utilize CO2. The first batch of products using the company’s technology are scheduled to enter the market in 2024.For all the promise of the carbon utilization industry, it remains to be seen if it can challenge the status quo. While Air Company started selling carbon-derived perfume in 2021, the startup has yet to build its first commercial plant, Sheehan says, citing the time-consuming process needed for collecting data and fine-tuning the technology for large-scale production.Fow now, the company’s demonstration facility in New York City — where CO2 and hydrogen gas flow through tubes into a reactor to form chemical reactions, aided by catalysts made from a confidential mixture of metals — is designed to yield at least 10,000 gallons of CO2-derived liquid annually. The limited production capacity has left many orders for its perfume — as well as jet fuels and Air Vodka, another popular product made from CO2 — unfilled.“We need to scale these facilities to the size of oil refineries today in order to have the impact on climate change that we want to have,” Sheehan says.
Article Summary: New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology.

Article Title: E-commerce firm Udaan raises $340 million ahead of planned IPO
Article Text: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain and boost vendor partnerships ahead of a stock market debut planned for 2025.The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt, the Bangalore-based company said in a statement Thursday. The round was led by M&G Plc and existing investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and DST Global participated.The round “fully funds our business plan,” Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan co-founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. “It enables our continued journey of growth and profitability, positioning us well to be public-market ready in the next 12-18 months.”Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, runs an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business, though a very small part of India’s overall retail market, is expected to swell to $150 billion in sales in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co.The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas, Gupta told Bloomberg News last month.Udaan was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran the company until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.
Article Summary: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain. The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt. The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas.

Article Title: Minuscule AI startup raises $41 million to tap India growth
Article Text: A generative artificial intelligence startup targeting the Indian market raised $41 million in fresh funding, the largest such round by an early-stage AI contender in the country.Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages at price points that the country’s 1.4 billion people can afford. The Series A funding round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, and participants included Silicon Valley billionaire Vinod Khosla’s Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners, formerly Sequoia Capital India & Southeast Asia, Sarvam said Thursday.The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems as well as tools for creating apps for the meager compute infrastructure available to developers in India. The startup has a total of 18 employees and is just opening an office in the city."What we are showing is that you can build large language models with limited resources,” Raghavan said in a phone interview. "We are building at a smaller scale and demonstrating that these can be extremely cost and energy efficient so they can be accessed by everyone."Large language models, like OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama, are powerful AI systems that understand by learning from vast amounts of diverse data from the internet and elsewhere to summarize, translate, and create text, audio and video for a wide range of applications. The rivalry to develop ever-more sophisticated models is heating up in Silicon Valley and such efforts have attracted billions of dollars in investments.
Article Summary: Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages. The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co- founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems.
